questions.q: What is the formula for a two-asset portfolio's variance?
questions.explain: Portfolio variance includes a cross term, 2*w1*w2*rho*sigma1*sigma2, that captures how the two assets move together — this is the term diversification benefit comes from.

questions.q: If two assets have a correlation of -1, what happens to the diversification benefit relative to assets with correlation +1?
options: There is no difference; correlation does not affect portfolio variance
The diversification benefit is maximized — the cross term becomes most negative, reducing portfolio variance the most
The portfolio becomes riskier than either asset alone in all cases
Correlation of -1 is not mathematically possible
questions.explain: Lower correlation shrinks the cross term in the variance formula; at rho = -1, the cross term is as negative as possible, which can in theory even allow full risk cancellation at the right weights.

questions.q: What is the key difference between systematic and unsystematic risk?
options: Systematic risk affects only bonds; unsystematic risk affects only stocks
Unsystematic risk is asset-specific and diversifiable by holding many assets; systematic risk is market-wide and cannot be diversified away
They are two names for the same concept
Systematic risk can always be reduced to zero with enough assets
questions.explain: Unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk tends to cancel out across many uncorrelated holdings. Systematic (market) risk affects all assets together and persists no matter how diversified the portfolio is.

questions.q: Two assets have sigma1 = 10%, sigma2 = 10%, equal weights of 0.5 each, and correlation rho = 1 (perfectly correlated). What is the portfolio's standard deviation?
questions.explain: With rho = 1, the portfolio variance formula collapses to (w1*sigma1 + w2*sigma2)^2, so sigma_p = w1*sigma1 + w2*sigma2 = 0.5*10% + 0.5*10% = 10% — no diversification benefit when correlation is perfect.

questions.q: Why do portfolio managers specifically look for assets with low or negative correlation to what they already hold, rather than just assets that are individually low-risk?
options: Low correlation has no effect on portfolio risk
Combining assets with low correlation reduces the cross term in the portfolio variance formula, producing a portfolio less risky than the weighted average of its individually-risky parts
Only negatively correlated assets are legal to hold together in a portfolio
Correlation only matters for bonds, not for equities
questions.explain: The diversification benefit comes specifically from the correlation term in the portfolio variance formula, not from each asset's individual risk level — even individually risky assets can combine into a lower-risk portfolio if their correlation is low enough.
